title: Bridges & Trusses
description: Our group designed, analyzed, and tested various truss structures to build two bridge prototypes, improving the design to increase load capacity from 2 kg to 10 kg while strengthening skills in truss analysis and iterative design.

timeline.heading: Objective
timeline.description: Our goal for this project was to build, test, and analyze 3 different popcicle truss structures (Warren, Howe, Pratt) to see which one could hold the most weight before breaking. Afterward, we would choose a truss design that would be used to build 2 full bridges, making improvements between both iterations. However, we were limited to use at most 80 popsicle sticks to build our bridges.

timeline.heading: Truss #1: Warren Truss
timeline.description: We first built the Warren Truss, which had a simple design based on the power of triangles. When we tested it, this truss only managed to hold around 6kg of weight, which made it the worst-performing bridge out of the three. Based on our truss analysis, we found that joints 3 and 5 had the greatest stress on it, so we thought that this joint would fail first. This truss experienced a joint failure at joints 3 and 5, which matched with our truss analysis.

timeline.heading: Truss #2: Howe Truss
timeline.description: We then built the Howe Truss. Compared to the Warren truss, there is a vertical beam supporting some of the vertical weight at joint 5, making that area more sturdy. We tested our design, which held around 13kg before the end of the truss broke, where we glued part of a popsicle stick since our truss ended up being too short. Our truss analysis found that the beam the weight is attached will break first, which didn't align with our testing. The truss could’ve held more weight if we had built the bridge properly.

timeline.heading: Truss #3: Pratt Truss
timeline.description: Our last truss was the Pratt truss, which we chose since it seemed similar to the Howe truss. We tested our bridge and found out that our bridge managed to hold around 19.75kg of weight before breaking. We did a truss analysis and found that the beam that which the weight was attached would break first, as the stress appears to be distributed between beams I & M. This aligned with the results from our testing.

timeline.heading: Truss Comparison and Selection
timeline.description: Based on the results, we chose the Pratt truss design for our bridge since it held the most weight before breaking. Also, we believe that beam failures are indicative of a better design compared to joint failures because joints tend to be weaker than beams, so if the beams fail, then that means our joints are as good as they can be, which was the case with the Pratt Truss.

timeline.heading: Bridge #1 Design and Construction
timeline.description: We made a quick sketch of the bridge based on the Pratt Truss and started building. A challenge we faced was figuring out how we wanted to connect both the trusses effectively. We were unsure of how we wanted to do so. We thought of just laying popsicle sticks across to attach them; however, Kevin thought that might’ve been too weak and wouldn’t be able to support the bridge well enough. So, we decided to cut slits on the top of the popsicle sticks to connect them.

timeline.heading: Bridge #1 Performance
timeline.description: Our bridge only held around 2.2kg before breaking, which was way less than the ~19kg it held before. After viewing the video, we realized the issue with the bridge wasn’t our truss, which stayed intact, but rather how we decided to connect them. The connection between the trusses was so weak that it caused the bridge to bend into an S shape, which made it unable to support a lot of weight. This eventually resulted in a Buckling in Compression Failure on the beams connecting the trusses.

timeline.heading: Bridge #2 Design and Construction
timeline.description: We kept our truss design mostly the same; however, according to our truss analysis, we found that 3 beams had no stress, so we got rid of them since they functionally did nothing. Also, we removed the top side of the bridge and instead directly connected the two trusses on the top to form a triangular cross-section, making the bridge more stable. We saved a lot of sticks by doing that, so we used all the saved sticks to connect the trusses on the bottom of the bridge, making the bridge even more stable.

timeline.heading: Bridge #2 Performance
timeline.description: Our bridge has a significant improvement in its load capacity as it held 10kg before breaking, more than the 2 kg it held before. This time, the connection between the 2 trusses managed to hold together well since the triangular shape of the cross section prevented the bridge from swaying and bending. However, the connections holding both ends of the bridge together broke, causing the ends to bend outwards and the bridge to fall. In future iterations of the bridge, the ends need to be further reinforced to prevent this from happening again.

timeline.heading: Final Thoughts
timeline.description: Overall, I learned a lot about bridge design from this project. One takeaway is that triangles are very powerful, as they can withstand a lot of force before breaking. This was really shown in our second iteration of our final bridge, as the triangular cross-section improved our bridge significantly. There were also a few triangles in our truss itself, which helped make the truss stronger. This idea can be applied outside of bridge design in designing structures. I gained a few skills from this project, like truss analysis, and improved my collaboration and teamwork skills. Our group worked well together throughout the project and successfully worked through the challenges together.
